title: Timers
lede: WHATWG/browser-standard timer functions as bare globals, matching real JS rather than a namespace. They are Node's own: Timeout and Immediate objects, timers of one duration sharing a list, one libuv timer armed for the earliest list, and immediates run in the loop's check phase after I/O; queueMicrotask has its own FIFO, drained after each callback.

entries.name: setTimeout(fn, ms) / clearTimeout(id)
entries.signature: setTimeout<TArgs extends any[]>(fn: (...args: TArgs) => void, ms?: number, ...args: TArgs): NodeJS.Timeout; clearTimeout(timeout: NodeJS.Timeout | string | number | undefined): void
entries.description: Schedules a callback to fire once after ms milliseconds passing it any arguments after ms, and returns an id; clearTimeout cancels it before it fires. These are bare global functions, matching real JS (not a namespace). Multiple timeouts fire in delay order, not registration order.

params.name: fn
params.desc: Callback; any function value, its result ignored.

params.name: args
params.desc: Arguments for fn, evaluated when the timer is scheduled.

returns.desc: Node's Timeout object: ref/unref/hasRef/refresh/close, and +timeout as its id, which clearTimeout also takes.

entries.name: setInterval(fn, ms) / clearInterval(id)
entries.signature: setInterval<TArgs extends any[]>(fn: (...args: TArgs) => void, ms?: number, ...args: TArgs): NodeJS.Timeout; clearInterval(id: NodeJS.Timeout | string | number | undefined): void
entries.description: Schedules a callback to repeat every ms milliseconds until cleared. Closures capture by reference, so the idiomatic self-cancelling pattern — a callback that reads the id its own declaration produces — works correctly. Same callback scope as setTimeout.

params.name: fn
params.desc: Callback; any function value, its result ignored.

params.name: args
params.desc: Arguments for fn on every tick, evaluated once at the schedule.

returns.desc: Node's Timeout object, usable with clearInterval.

entries.name: setImmediate(fn) / clearImmediate(id)
entries.signature: setImmediate<TArgs extends any[]>(fn: (...args: TArgs) => void, ...args: TArgs): NodeJS.Immediate; clearImmediate(immediate: NodeJS.Immediate | undefined): void
entries.description: Schedules a callback for the loop's check phase, after I/O polling, as Node does: scheduled from an I/O callback it runs before a 0 ms setTimeout.

params.name: fn
params.desc: Callback; any function value, its result ignored.

params.name: args
params.desc: Arguments for fn, evaluated when the immediate is scheduled.

returns.desc: Node's Immediate object: ref/unref/hasRef, usable with clearImmediate.

entries.name: queueMicrotask(fn)
entries.description: Queues a callback onto a real microtask FIFO, distinct from the timer queue, drained after the synchronous script and before any timers fire.

entries.name: timers/promises
entries.signature: setTimeout<T = void>(delay?: number, value?: T, options?: TimerOptions): Promise<T>; setImmediate<T = void>(value?: T, options?: TimerOptions): Promise<T>; setInterval<T = void>(delay?: number, value?: T, options?: TimerOptions): AsyncGenerator<T>
entries.description: The promise forms of the timers. setTimeout and setImmediate resolve with their value; setInterval is an async iterator that yields its value on every tick until the loop breaks. An AbortSignal in options rejects the pending timer with an AbortError, and ref: false lets the process exit while it waits. scheduler.wait and scheduler.yield are setTimeout and setImmediate without a value.

params.name: value
params.desc: What the promise resolves with, or the iterator yields.

params.name: options
params.desc: { signal?: AbortSignal, ref?: boolean }, validated as Node does.

returns.desc: Settles when the timer fires or its signal aborts.

entries.snippet:
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'timers/promises'
console.log(await sleep(10, 'kalimera'))
